opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When we say "world foundation model," we're really borrowing from two ideas.

The first is the "foundation model" part. Over the last few years, we've seen that if you train a large model on a huge amount of diverse data, you get something general-purpose that people can then fine-tune for many downstream tasks. Language models showed this very clearly. You don't train one model for translation and another for summarization; you train one big model and adapt it.

The second is the "world model" part. A world model is a model that understands how the physical world evolves. If I give it the current state of the world, say a video of what's happening right now, plus some action, like a robot moving its arm or a car turning left, it can predict what happens next. It's essentially a simulator learned from data rather than hand-coded with physics equations.

Cosmos combines these. We train on a very large amount of video, millions of hours covering driving, robotics, human activity, nature, so the model learns general knowledge about physics, objects, motion and cause and effect. That's the foundation. Then a developer building, say, a humanoid robot or an autonomous vehicle can take Cosmos and post-train it on their own smaller dataset to get a world model specialized for their robot, their cameras, their environment.

The reason we think this matters is that physical AI has a data problem. For language you can scrape the internet. For robots, collecting real-world interaction data is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. If you have a good world model, you can generate synthetic experience, evaluate policies, and let the AI "imagine" outcomes before acting in the real world. So Cosmos is meant to be the base layer that the whole physical AI community can build on, which is also why we made it open. We want it to be a starting point, not an endpoint.

r001.rationale: The response describes Cosmos as a shared base layer that developers can post-train on their own data to create world models tailored to their robots, vehicles, and environments.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as Ming-Yu Liu, drawing only on the conversation so far.

Thank you for having me. We call Cosmos a world foundation model because of what it is trying to learn, which is not language, and not just images or video as pixels, but the dynamics of the physical world itself. A language model learns how words follow words. A world model learns how the world evolves: if a robot arm pushes a cup, the cup slides and maybe tips over; if a car turns left at an intersection, the scene in front of it changes in a particular way; objects stay solid, light behaves consistently, gravity pulls things down. Those regularities are what we want the model to internalize.

The "foundation" part is about generality and reuse. The way GPT-style models became a base layer that many applications are built on, we want Cosmos to be a base layer for physical AI, meaning robots, autonomous vehicles, anything that has to perceive and act in the real world. Training a model from scratch for every robot, every embodiment, every environment is incredibly expensive, and the data is scarce. So instead we pre-train on an enormous amount of video of the physical world, so the model picks up a general understanding of physics, geometry, motion, and cause and effect. Then developers can fine-tune it for their specific robot or driving stack with much less data.

Practically, that gives you a few things. You can use it as a simulator: give it the current state and an action, and it predicts what happens next, so you can generate synthetic training data or test a policy in situations that are too rare or too dangerous to collect in reality. You can also use it as a kind of mental model inside the agent, so the robot can imagine the consequences of an action before taking it, which is how humans plan too.

So the phrase is really a statement of intent. Language models gave us a foundation for digital intelligence. Cosmos is our attempt at a foundation for intelligence that has to live in, and understand, the physical world. We also open-sourced it because we think the physical AI community needs a shared starting point, the same way the language community had one.

r001.rationale: It describes Cosmos as a reusable base layer and shared starting point that developers can fine-tune for specific robots or driving systems.

astra-6.text:
We call Cosmos a world foundation model because the goal is to model how the physical world evolves. A language model predicts the next token; a world model predicts what might happen next in a scene, given what it has observed and potentially an action. That requires understanding things like motion, spatial relationships, and physical interactions.

The word “foundation” is important because we want that capability to support many downstream tasks. For physical AI, such as robots or autonomous vehicles, a model of the world can help generate scenarios and anticipate the consequences of actions. So the goal goes beyond producing a realistic video—it’s to provide a foundation for systems that need to operate in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response says Cosmos should support many downstream tasks and serve as a foundation for physical AI systems, but does not explain that others can build world models tailored to their own uses from this shared foundation.

sol-6.1.text:
We call Cosmos a world foundation model because it is designed to learn how the physical world evolves. A language model predicts the next token; a world model predicts what might happen next in a scene—how objects move, interact, and respond to actions.

The “foundation” part means that this capability can support many different tasks. For example, you can condition a model on observations and actions to generate possible future scenarios, which can help with training and evaluating robots or autonomous vehicles. The goal is to provide a general foundation for physical AI.

r001.rationale: The response describes Cosmos as a general foundation for physical AI that supports many tasks, but does not say it is a shared foundation others use to build world models tailored to their own uses.
